Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development in its Fifth Report on Demands for Grants for 1994-95 of Department of
Education (Demand No. 47) has recommended enhancement/increase in allocation of funds
in respect of Elementary Education (Para 24), Teacher Education (para 37), Secondary
Education (Para 39), Vocational Education (para 42), Computer Education (para 44),
Scholarships (para 47), Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (para 49), Novodaya Vidyalayas (para
59), Environmental Awareness (para 65), University & Higher Education (paras 66 & 69),
Indian Council of Philosophical Research (para 81), Central Universities (paras 84 & 85),
Language Development (Paras 94, 95 & 99) and Technical Education (paras 101 & 105).
The Committee has in essence recommended increased allocation of resources for the
education sector itself since sectoral recommendations cover the entire range of educational
activities.

2. From 1968 onwards, when the First National Plan on Education was formulated on
the basis of Kothari Commission Report, the goal has been to set apart 6% of the National
Income for Education. This goal was reiterated by the National Policy on Education, 1986.
In the “Education for All” (EFA) of Nine High Population Countries held in Delhi on 16th
December, 1993, the Prime Minister declared the Commitment of the country to reach the
target of 6% of GNP by the turn of the century. This commitment was reiterated in the
Conference of Chief Ministers held as a follow-up of the EFA-9 Summit on 15th February,
1994,

3, Investment in education is in a large measure through public funds made available by
the Central and State Governments. Besides Education Department, other Departments also
spend on Education. This expenditure amounted to Rs. 4406 crores in 1992-93. Apart from
plan and non plan allocations additional avenues for raising resources for education are
being explored in the form of Educational Cess and exempting donation to Educational
Institutions from Income Tax. Chief Ministers have also decided to explore ways to enhance
resources for Education. In addition investment in education by the local bodies and by
private individuals/trust have also to be considered.

4. The policy postulates made in the National Policy on Education, subsequent
commitments made during EFA Summit and Chief Ministers’ Conference and trend of
enhanced allocation during various Plans generate the confidence that the target of
allocation of 6% GNP for Education would be reached by the end of Ninth Five Year Plan.
The Department of Education is making efforts to seek additional plan allocation every year
so that sectoral allocations could inerease. Actual inter-se increases in allocation would
depend upon the extent of the total increase within the priority framework of the
Department i.e. the highest priority to elementary education and literacy. In keeping with
the recommendations made by the Standing Committee last year, the Department ensured
the following step up in allocation to the schemes commended by the Committee.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN  
ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
III.  INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICE (ICDS) SCHEME  
Special intervention for construction of AWC building  
Recommendations/Observations  
3.5.3 Short working season, non-availability of con struction materials at site, difficult terrain and carriage by head loads in 
remote locations, low capacity of village-based con tractor are the main factors cited as responsible f or this state of affairs. The 
Committee while appreciating the region-specific co nstraints of North - East States would like to poin t out that urgent steps 
need to be taken by the Centre in co-ordination wit h the State Governments so as to resolve/lessen the se problem areas. The 
Committee also strongly feels that local community along with PRIs may be motivated like the Young Miz o Association in 
Mizoram for taking part in this exercise. The Commi ttee also recommends that this over-delayed constru ction work of AWC 
buildings may be got completed in a time-bound manner.  
Action Taken  
  The matter has been taken up with the NER states for completion of all the AWC buildings sanctioned till 2009-10 in the 
State Secretaries Review Meeting held on 28th October, 2010. It was also clarified to the NE states th at further funds would be 
released only after completion certificates are rec eived. This has also been followed up through a D.O . letter dated 2nd 
November, 2010 from the Ministry to all the Secreta ries of NE States urging them to furnish pending DC  and progress of 
construction of AWCs. 
Recommendations/Observations  
3.5.4  The Committee has been emphasizing on infras tructure development of AWCs with special reference  to construction of 
AWC building in the past. Majority of AWCs do not h ave their own building. The Committee was informed that the Planning 
Commission in its Review Meeting of ICDS held on 13th and 20th November, 2009 had suggested that appropriate investments 
in infrastructure at the AWC level needed to be explored. The Ministry had also requested the Thirteenth Finance Commission’ 
to provide for the construction of Anganwadi Centres in the State allocation and a decision was awaited. While appreciating the 
efforts of the Ministry, the Committee would like t o draw its attention to the fact that the Report of  the Thirteenth Finance 
Commission had already been presented to the Parlia ment. If the proposal has not been recommended by t he Commission, the 
Committee strongly feels that the Ministry needs to  approach the Planning Commission so as to ensure t hat this proposal is 
substantially included in the approach to the Twelfth Five Year Plan. 
Action Taken  
  The 13th Finance Commission has recommended const ruction of AWCs with an estimated cost of Rs. 1982 Crore in six 
states which demanded for it, namely Chhattisgarh ( Rs.l50 Crore), Jharkhand (Rs.432 Crore), Madhya Pradesh (Rs.400 Crore), 
Maharashtra (Rs.300 Crore), Orissa (Rs.400 Crore) and West Bengal (Rs.300 Crore). 
  Construction of AWC building as an activity was p roposed in the XI Five Year Plan, but could not be approved by GOI. 
However, in the Mid-Term Appraisal for the XI Five Year Plan, Planning Commission has recommended adeq uate 
infrastructure for AWCs. The issue of construction will be pursued in XII Five Year Plan. 
VI.  INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.6  Committee’s attention has been drawn by the Mo del Rules framed under the Juvenile Justice (Care a nd Protection of 
Children) Act, 2000 which provide for constitution of Inspection Committees by the State Governments /  UTs at State, District 

or City Level. These Committees are required to vis it and oversee the conditions of the institutions/h omes and appropriateness 
of the processes for safety, well being, review the standards of care and protection, look into the functioning of the Management 
Committee and Children’s Committee and give suggest ions for improvement. The Committee finds that the Inspection 
Committees are being set up by the respective State  Governments under ICPS. The Committee apprehends t hat so far this very 
important monitoring mechanism envisaged under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 was not 
there in position or not effective, if existing in majority of the States. The Committee strongly feel s that in the absence of 
constant and rigorous monitoring, the very objectiv e. If all such homes, i.e. , protection of vulnerable children would remain on  
paper inspite of lofty schemes and substantive fund ing. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Centre has to play a 
pro-active role in getting the real sense. The Committee would appreciate if publicity to services provided by these Child Lines 
is given in the cities from where these are operating on a regular basis through both print and electronic media. 
Action Taken  
  To strengthen the monitoring mechanisms of the St ate Governments further, provision has been made un der the 
Integrated Child Protection Scheme for supervision and monitoring of all child care organizations/ institutions/ agencies, at both 
State and District levels. The Programme Manager (Child Protection) of the State Child Protection Society at the State level and 
the Protection Officer (Institutional Care) under D istrict Child Protection Society, at the District l evel, have been given the 
responsibilty to ensure supervision and monitoring all the institutions/agencies housing children in t he State and ensure 
implementation of minimum standards of care. 
  Publicity to the Child line services is being pro vided both through the electronic and print media from time to time. Child 
line India Foundation, Mumbai is also undertaking p ublicity and awareness campaigns in the cities wher e Child line service is 
available. 
VII.  SCHEME OF HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN 
Recommendations/Observations  
7.7  The Committee would like to draw the attention  of the Ministry towards areas where there are nume rous industries 
forming an industrial hub but there are no provisio n of hostels for working women due to which women d o not opt to work in 
such areas which offer ample employment opportunities to them. Further, only 887 hostels sanctioned do  not cater to the needs 
of all the working women across the country. Therefore, the Committee recommends that additional hostels for working women 
should be sanctioned especially in areas left uncovered so that more and more number of women are benefited from the scheme. 
Action Taken  
  Recommendation of Hon’ble Committee has been note d for compliance. 
IX.   RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK) 
Recommendations/Observations  
9.4   In view of restructuring of RMK, the Committe e would like to point out that the need of the hour  is to focus on better 
management of the portfolio of the poor women and i mproving the overall chain which converts the viabl e ones into genuine 
women entrepreneurs. Micro-finance organizations should identify the needs of the poor women, their saving capacity and time 
period and mode of repayment of loan. It is time to explore more about the whole philosophy of micro financing and successful 
experiences in the international context. 
Action Taken  
  The suggestions made by the Committee have been t aken note of. 
XI.   CONCLUSION 
Recommendations/Observations  

15.1  The Committee while reviewing the allocation, utilization trends and performance of various schemes administered by the 
Ministry, finds that utilization of allocated funds  has been more or less satisfactory. The Ministry, however, needs to monitor 
the implementation of schemes as many schemes could not accomplish their set targets, with special focus on the implementing 
agencies like the NGOs. The target groups of the sc hemes of the Ministry are women and children and th ey are the most 
vulnerable section of our society and they need to be addressed with utmost care and sensitivity. The Ministry needs to lay 
emphasis on the timely implementation of its new sc hemes and the revamping of the schemes under proces s. The Committee 
believes that concerted efforts of the Ministry wou ld certainly lead to the evolution of an efficient delivery mechanism with 
minimum hindrances. 
Action Taken  
  The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee have  been noted for compliance.

II.   BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendations/observations  
2.1   Eleventh Plan allocation of Rs. 56,765,00 cro re for the Ministry shows almost five times enhance ment when compared 
with the Tenth Plan allocation of Rs.12,018.22 cror e. When compared with final Tenth Plan expenditure figures of 
Rs.13,073.70 crore. Eleventh Plan allocation can be  consid ered 4.5 times higher. Against an allocatio n of Rs. 20343.00 crore 
during the first three years of the plan period, expenditure reported upto 22nd March, 2010 was Rs.20,143.97 crore. 
Action Taken  
  No comments. 
Recommendations/observations  
2.2   Plan allocation of Rs. 7350.00 crore for 2009 -10 was enhanced to Rs.8550.00 crore at the RE stag e. By the end of the 
year (22nd March,2010) utilization figure reflected 97.45 per cent RE provision. The Committee notes that allocation for 2010-
11 has been further enhanced to Rs. 11000.00 crore, showing a 49.66 per cent increase over 2009-10 BE provision. 
Action Taken  
  No comments. 
Recommendations/observations  
2.3  The Committee was informed that allocation of Rs.11000. 00 crore for 2010-11 falls short of proje cted requirement of 
Rs.16901.97 crore with major gap being in Rashtriya  Mahila Kosh (allocation ofRs.15.00 crore against a  requirement of 
Rs.100.00 crore), ICDS (allocation of Rs.8700.00 cr ore against a requirement of Rs.11,227.00 crore) IC PS (Rs.300.00 crore

Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent G irls (Rs.1000.00 crore against a projection of Rs.2 107.00 crore) and 
Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana (Rs.390.00 crore against a requirement of Rs.2217.18 crore). The Committee, however, 
notes that the fund allocation for these new schemes has been made at an enhanced level when compared with 2009-10. 
  While appreciating the genuine requirements and t rack-record of optimum utilization of funds in well -established 
schemes like ICDS, the Committee would like to poin t out that with respect to schemes yet to be approv ed, the Ministry has to 
primarily focus on getting the schemes approved expeditiously by the competent authority.  
Action Taken  
  Serious efforts have been made to get the new sch emes approved in the year. Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of 
Adolescent Girls (RGSEAG) has been approved by the Govt. on the pilot scale for 200 districts in the c ountry. It has been 
launched on 19.11.2010. Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahy og Yojana (IGMSY) was approved by the CCEA in its m eeting held on 
20.10.2010. 
  Keeping in view the fact that Ministry of Rural D evelopment has launched a big programme to involve all the BPL 
families in SHGs and also in view of the comments r eceived from the Planning Commission, it has been d ecided not to pursue 
the Swayamsidha Scheme. 
  As for the lower allocation in 2010-11 against pr ojected requirement, request for additional allocat ion at RE stage has

of Action Plan of 2009-10 and its inability to carr y out its most important function i.e. of facilitating adoptions. The Committee 
hopes that with the post of Secretary being filled up and the Action Plan ready for the year 2010-11, CARA would be able to 
utilize the allocated funds and the year 2010-11 would witness an increase of inter-country and in-country adoptions. 
Action Taken  
  The number of adoptions during a year depends on various factors like availability of children who a re legally free for 
adoption, availability of such children in Govt. recognized adoption agencies, number of prospective adoptive parents available, 
expeditious adoption orders by the Court. 
  There is a fall in the adoption figures as report ed by CARA due to the fact that a larger number of children are being 
placed through direct adoption by hospitals, nursin g homes and other such institutions not recognized by the Govt. as adoption 
agencies. As such adoptions do not proceed through Govt. recognized adoption agencies, there is no mec hanism to assess the 
exact number of adoptions that have taken place during the year. 
  The Action Plan for 2010-11 has been approved by the Management Committee of CARA in its meeting on 3rd May 
2010 and CARA would be able to achieve its targets for the year and also utilize the funds allocated for 2010-11.

  The Committee in its previous Report had highligh ted the issue of unspent balances with State Govern ments and had 
recommended that the matter of unspent balances should be urgently taken up with the concerned State Governments so that the 
implementation of an important scheme like ICDS is not hampered. The Ministry has to constantly monitor specially in view of 
substantive enhancement of funds for ICDS. 
Action Taken  
  As per the instructions of Ministry of Finance, g rants under ICDS are released in four or more insta llments in a year. The 
first two installments are released on indicative b asis (based on norms, number of beneficiaries, oper ational projects and 
operational AWCs). Subsequent installments are rele ased on the basis of Statement of Expenditure as on  30th June and 30th 
September. Any unspent balance or excess expenditur e reported as on 31st March in a particular year is  adjusted in the 
following financial year.  

  The indication of balance on 31st December is par t of releases & expenditure made upto 3rd quarter a nd part of a 
continuous process. It is therefore not considered as ‘unspent balance’ for the purpose of release of funds during the financial 
year. The actual position of excess expenditure/uns pent balance as on 31.3.2010 (Annex 1)  will be taken into account and 
adjusted while releasing grants in 3rd installment of current year. 
  For example: In the case of Uttar Pradesh, the St ate had Rs.67.95 Cr. available with them as on 31.12.2009 out of the first 
three installments. However, as on 31.3.2010 there was an unspent balance of Rs.47.18 crore only under  ICDS(General). This 
has been adjusted from the amount due for releasing 3rd installment of funds to Uttar Pradesh in the year 2010-11. 
  Similarly in the case of Gujarat, the State made an excess expenditure 24.62 crores as on 31.3.2010 which was adjusted 
while releasing 3rd installment to Gujarat in the year 2010-11. 
  The balances with State Governments (Plus or Minu s) are therefore, not taken up with State Governments on the basis of 
availability of funds with them as on 31.12.2009. H owever, the States are exhorted to submit Statement  of Expenditure timely 
for the purpose of financial progress. 
Comments of the Committee 
  The Committee does not wish to be drawn in techni cal/procedural formalities pertaining to pendency o f unspent 
balances. Committee’s prime concern is for implemen tation of a major programme meant for children in a  judicious 
manner as per the envisaged norms and action plan. States-wise excess expenditure/unspent balance as o n 31 March, 
2010 confirms Committee’s justified concern. There are states like Gujarat (Rs. 24.61 crore), Haryana (Rs. 67.92 crore), 
Jharkhano (Rs. 47.37 crore), Kerala (Rs. 44.07 cror e), Tamil Nadu (Rs. 39.27 crore), West Bengal (Rs. 74.60 crore) 
which have incurred excess expenditure. In contrast , States like Bihar (Rs. 13.11 crore), Orissa (Rs. 28.50 crore), 
Rajasthan (Rs. 18.32 crore), Uttar Pradesh (Rs. 47.18 crore), Assam (Rs. 26.28 crore) and Nagaland (Rs. 16.22 crore) are 
having unspent balance. Either way, it can be concl uded that the Flagship Scheme of ICDS is both not r eaching all its 
targeted beneficiaries and not being implemented as  per the financia1 norms. The Committee, therefore,  reiterates that

Recommendations/Observations  
3.1  ICDS is the most important flagship scheme of the Ministry which seeks to provide a package of se rvices comprising of 
supplementary nutrition, immunization, health check up and referral services, pre-school non formal education for children upto 
six years of age, pregnant and lactating mothers. I n the recent past, the Ministry has undertaken the task of universalisation of 
the Scheme by increasing the number of AWCs to 14 l akh with a provision of 20,000 AWCs on demand with special focus on 
coverage of SC/ST population. Cost sharing has been introduced between Centre and State, from 2009-10 in the ratio 90: 10 for 
all components including SNP for North-East and 50: 50 for SNP and 90:10 for all other components for a ll States other than 
North-East. Enhancement of honorarium for AWWs/Help ers, provision of Flexi funds at Anganwadi level, r eward mechanism 
for ICDS functionaries are some of the major interventions made under ICDS. 
  The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Mini stry in making the delivery mechanism more effectiv e by taking such 
interventions. The Committee hopes that all these i nitiatives of the Ministry would have a positive im pact on the 
operationalization and effective functioning of AWCs in all the States/UTs, specially those not performing well.  
Action Taken  
  It is expected that the impetus now being given t o the ICDS Scheme would have a positive impact on t he performance of 
the scheme in all the states. With continuous efforts and regular monitoring, the number of operational AWCs/mini-AWCs have 
increased from 11,04,262 in December,2009 to 11,95,256 on 30.9.2010. 
  The number of AWWs in-position have been increase d from 10,95,298 in May 2010 to 11,18,025 as on 30t h September 
2010 and helpers increased from 10,64,657 to 10,84,786 during the same period. 

  The issue of Universalisation of ICDS and filling  up of vacancies of ICDS functionaries was taken up  with States/UTs 
during the State Ministers & Secretaries Meeting he ld on 16-17 June, 2010 and with Secretaries of Stat es on 28th 
October,2010.States have informed that the delay in  filling up of vacancies is on account of delay in Sanction, Processing, 
Selection Committee and recruitment including court  cases. States/UTs have been asked to expedite the matter which may 
include taking up the matter suitably with the Court. 
  State-wise details as on 30th September 2010 is g iven at Annexure-II. 
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Mini stry in increasing the number of operational AWCs/mini-AWCs 
from 11,04,262 in December, 2009 to 11,95,256 on 30  September, 2010. Similar increase in the in-positi on AWWs & 
AWHs has been witnessed. However, the Committee notes the vacancy position in the States with respect to supervisors, 
AWWs & AWHs with maximum vacancies found in Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The Committee observes that prolonged 
process of recruitment and court cases are the two main factors responsible for a large number of post s of ICDS 
functionaries remaining vacant. The Committee has been given to understand that the issue of filling u p of vacancies of  
ICDS functionaries and issue of universalisation of  ICDS was taken up with States/UTs during the State  Ministers 
meetings held on 16-17 June, 2010 and with Secretaries of States on 28 October, 2010. The Committee is also of the view 
that these issues need to be taken up with the conc erned State Governments at the highest level so as to expedite the 
filling up of the vacant posts. 
Recommendations/Observations  
3.2.4  From 2009-10, cost sharing between Centre and States has been introduced in the ratio of 90:10 for all other components 
for all States other than North-East. On a specific  query about States’ acceptance of the revised norm s, the Committee was 
informed that State Government of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir have requested that they may be treated at par 
with North-East States for 90: 10 considering their topographic conditions. The Committee strongly feels that the requests of the 
two States i.e.  of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir regarding treating them at par with North-Eastern States for 90:10 
contribution considering their topographic conditions, need to be looked into in the proper perspectiv e and the needful done at 
the earliest. 
Action Taken  
  In view of the difficult climatic conditions and terrain, the Planning Commission has been requested  on 12.2.2010 
followed by five reminders to indicate the present trend of ratio of cost sharing in respect of three States, namely, Jammu & 
Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and also in addition, Uttarakhand, that whether it is at par with NE States or otherwise. This would 
facilitate further consideration of the requests of  3 States by the Ministry and taking it up with Min istry of Finance. The 
information is awaited. This is being followed up with the Planning Commission.  
Comments of the Committee 
  The Committee is of the view that the issue of co st sharing basis under ICDS Scheme for Jammu & Kash mir, 
Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand on the pattern of North-Eastern States needs to be decided and implemented at the 
earliest. 
Universalisation of ICDS 
Recommendations/Observations  
3.3.1  The ICDS scheme has been expanded in three p hases in 2005-06, 2006-07 and 2008-09. During the t hird phase of 
expansion, 792 additional projects and 2,13,859 AWC s and 77,102 Mini AWCs and provision for 20,000 Ang anwadi on 
Demand have been approved in October, 2008. With th is approval, cumulative total of approved projects and Anganwadi 
Centres increased to 7076 and 14 lakh, thus fulfill ing the directions of Supreme court for universalis ation of lCDS. Committee 
was given to understand that some States reduced th eir requirements for AWCs subsequent to approval by  the Government. 

Eventually the cumulative total of sanctioned AWCs/ Mini AWCs as on 31st March, 2009 is 13.56 lakh. The  remaining 44,000 
AWCs/Mini AWCs, including 20,000 Anganwadis on Demand are yet to be sanctioned. Not only this, requests have come from 
some States for further reduction. 
Action Taken  
  As on 30.9.2010, the total number of sanctioned A WCs is 13.67 lakh. The Ministry is left with the ba lance of 36,721 
AWCs. This includes 20,000 anganwadi on Demand. 
  The Ministry has received requests for down scali ng of AWCs from the States of Chhatisgarh [surrende ring 11,946 
AWCs out of 20,772 sanctioned by GOl under 3rd Phase of expansion] and Uttrakhand [surrendering 3,195 out of 8,375 AWCs 
sanctioned under the 3rd Phase of expansion]. 
  Further, requests for sanctioning of a total 16,7 34 AWCs have been received from 10 States. The matt er is under 
consideration of the Ministry.  
Recommendations/Observations  
3.3.2 The Committee fails to comprehend the basis for this reversal in the requirement for AWCs in respect of some States. Not 
only this, Supreme Court’s directions for universal isation of ICDS thereby opening of 14 lakh AWCs wer e based on an 
extensive survey as per the prescribed population n orms along with State-specific requirements. In suc h a scenario, request of 
some States for reduction not only goes against the Apex Court directions but also seems to negate the very objective of ICDS. 
Action Taken  
  The Anganwadi Centers are to be opened as per the  population norms prescribed by the Governinent of India. The States 
of Chhatisgarh and Uttrakhand have approached the M inistry for reduction in the number of AWCs and hav e stated that they 
have revisited the survey conducted earlier and there is a need for reduction in the number of AWCs/Mini-AWCs. 
  The Government of india has, upon this, re-direct ed these States to certify that the revised require ment of AWCs/Mini-
AWCs is as per population norms and that with the sanction and operationalisation of these AWCs/Mini-AWCs each and every, 
habitation in the State, will be covered under ICDS as per norms. 
  The reduction in the number of AWCs/Mini-AWCs by these two States may not violate the directions of Supreme Court 
as the balance AWCs would be available for sanction, if required, by other States. 
Recommendations/Observations  
3.3.3  The Committee was informed by the Secretary that Chhattisgarh and Uttrakhand were the two States which had asked for 
substantive reduction. The Committee is happy to no te that the request of these two States has not bee n agreed to so far. The 
Committee feels that revision in the cost norms may  perhaps be one reason for this development. The Co mmittee recommends 
that the Ministry should pursue this issue with the concerned States vigorously so that no habitation in these two States remains 
bereft of positive gains of ICDS. 
Action Taken  
  The States of Chhatisgarh and Uttrakhand have app roached the Ministry for reduction in the number of  AWCs on the 
ground that they have revisited the survey conducte d earlier and there is a need for reduction in the number of AWCs/mini-
AWCs. 
  However, Government is not aware that revision in  cost norms is one of the reasons for downscaling t he number of 
AWCs. 
  The Govt. of India has reiterated its directions to certify that the revised requirement of AWCs/Min i-AWCs is as per 
population norms and that with the sanction and operationalisation of these AWCs/Mini-AWCs each and every habitation in the 
State will be covered under ICDS as per norms and saturating SC/ST & Minority Habitations. 

Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry in  re-directing the States of Chhatisgarh & Uttarakha nd to 
certify that the revised requirement of AWCs/mini-A WCs is as per population norms and that with the sa nction and 
operationalisation of these AWCs/mini-AWCs, each an d every habitation in the State, will be covered un der ICDS as 
per norms. The Committee would like to be apprised about the response of these States or any certificate received so far 
in this regard. The Committee is of the view that i f revision in cost norms is not the reason for down scaling the number 
of AWCs, the real reasons for putting up such a request for down scaling of AWCs need to be identified.

Recommendations/Observations  
3.3.7  The issue of outreach of ICDS not reaching a ll the targeted beneficiaries was raised by some of  the members. It was 
pointed out that AWCs at present have been opened a t Panchayat level only in States like Madhya Prades h. Normally, 
jurisdiction of a Panchayat extends upto a number o f villages. As a result, pregnant women and small c hildren, finding it 
difficult to cover the distance between the AWC at Panchayat and villages covered’ by it remain depriv ed of Supplementary 
Nutrition. Similarly, attention of the Ministry was also drawn to women workforce working in tea gardens and their children not 
getting the benefit of ICDS. Population norms of 800 for one AWCs or minimum requirement of habitations having 40 children 
were not helping the labour population, e.g.  those employed for sugarcane harvesting or very small habitations of labourers and 
uneducated class having less than 40 children. The Committee strongly feels that all the problem areas  pointed out by the 
Members, based on their first hand experience of gr ound realities need to be looked into immediately. The Committee would 
appreciate if a survey of these areas as well as ot her similar areas is be taken up by the Ministry in  co-ordination with the 
concerned States. Present norm of 40 children for A nganwadis on Demand may also be reviewed, specially  in case of specific 
demands for relaxation of the same. 
Action Taken  
  In order to cover 14 lakh habitations across the country and also the hitherto uncovered habitations  including SC/ST and 
Minority habitations, Govt. of India revised the po pulation norms for setting up of AWCs. The lowest p opulation norm is 150-
300 for setting up of a Mini-AWC and highest is 400 -800 for setting up of AWC. If there are habitation s having less than 40 
children, these are likely to be covered by the population norms prescribed by the Govt. of India which may include tea gardens 
and other far-flung topographically difficult areas. 
  During 3rd Phase of expansion of ICDS, the State of Madhya Pradesh was sanctioned 86 additional ICDS  Projects (61-
Rural, 19- Tribal and 6- Urban), 9691 AWCs and 9820  mini-AWCs vide  Ministry’s letter No. 14-212008-CD-I dated 
17.12.2008. 
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee is constrained to take note of the response of the Ministry to specific problem areas with regard to 
location of AWCs in some States which were noticed by the Members. Instead of exploring the feasibilit y of setting up 
AWCs as per the requirements of local population, the Ministry has chosen to give a very general reply. The Committee 
would like to point out that if targeted beneficiar ies remain deprived of the facilities available und er the scheme, the 
issue of sanctioned and operational AWCs would remain confined to academic exercise only. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates that specific problem areas as enumerate d by the Members need to be looked into without any  further delay. 
The Committee is of the view that the outreach of ICDS should be extended to every habitation and groups so that more 
and more women and children benefit from the scheme . The viability of AWCs with special components to cater to the 
needs of women workforce working in tea gardens or residing in far flung topographically difficult are as should be 
explored so that local specificity of the State and population is taken into consideration. 

Recommendations/Observations 
Pre-School Education Kits  
3.4.1 Pre-school Education is a critical component under the ICDS Scheme to ensure the holistic development of children. Pre-
School Education Kits are procured and supplied by StateslUts as per norms. To strengthen this component of ICDS, cost norms 
for these kits have been revised from Rs.500 to Rs. 1000 per AWC per annum from 2009-10. The Committee is, however, 
surprised to note that State-wise status of procurement of Pre-School Kits for AWCs in 2008-09 and 200 9-10 reveals that large 
number of States/UTs i.e.  Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Jharkhand, Kerala, 
Maharashtra, Chandigarh, Delhi, Puducherry, Meghala ya, Mizoram and Sikkim have so far failed to provid e this vital 
component to the children in AWCs in their States/U Ts. What is more disturbing is that in State slUTs like Chhattisgarh, 
Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, C handigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Delhi, Arunachal  Pradesh and 
Tripura, procurement process for the Kits is continuing for long. In Maharashtra, Kits for 2009-10 as well as 2008-09 are being 
procured. In respect of the remaining States, numbe r of procured kits for 2009-10 falls short of the r equirement or no response 
has been forthcoming so far.  
Recommendations/Observations  
3.4.2  The Committee is very disappointed with this state of affairs. It seems that States are not int erested in procuring the Pre-
school Education Kits for their Children. The Commi ttee would like to point out that these kits are a replacement for pre-
parental education in nursery school. They can be c onsidered an important tool for enhancing literacy at the end of class-V. 
World-wide, it is an established fact that children  having a certain minimum vocabulary before enterin g school have a higher 
chance of achieving literacy at the end of class V.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that concerte d efforts need to be 
made so as to convince the States to include this v ery crucial component financial assistance for whic h is provided by the 
Centre. 
Action Taken 3.4.1 & 3.4.2  
  The States/UTs have been requested to procure the  Pre-School Kits for Anganwadi Centres regularly. A  detailed report 
has been sought from the States/UTs regarding procu rement status for the year 2009-10 and the plan for  2010-11. The matter 
was raised in the review meeting held on 16-17 June  2010 with the States/UTs. The State/UTs were urged  to make the 
Anganwadi Centres more attractive and joyful for th e children and ensure availability of PSE kits at a ll Anganwadi Centres. 
They were also advised to use more and more local m aterials and effective communication for making lea rning joyful for the 
children. 
  The status of procurement of Medicine Kits and Pr e-School Education Kits for the year, 2008-09 and 2 009-10 is at 
Annex-III . There is no progress in procurement of Pre-School  Kits in any of the States/UTs. The matter was agai n taken up 
with the States/UTs in the State Secretaries Review Meeting held on 28th October, 2010. 
Comments of the Committee 
  The Committee is dismayed to note the state of af fairs of procurement of Pre-school Education Kits a nd Medicine 
Kits. The Committee has been informed that procurement process is under process in eleven States for the year 2009-10. 
No information has been received from the States li ke Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir,  
Jharkhand, Lakshadweep, Puducherry and Sikkim for t he year 2009-10. In States/Uts like Chhattisgarh, K arnataka, 
Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Delhi, Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura, 
procurement process for both Medicine Kits and Pre-school Education Kits in 2009-10 is still going on. Status of 2010-11 
has not been made available to the Committee. Only one State and Union Territory i.e  Assam and Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands procured kits as per requirement of operational AWCs. The Committee has been informed by the M inistry that 
inspite of their efforts, there has been no progress in procurement of Pre-school Education Kits in any of the States/UTs. 
The matter was last taken up with the States/UTs in the State Secretaries Review Meeting held on 28 October, 2010. The 
Committee would like to reiterate that the Ministry  should take up the matter again with the States at  the highest level 
for strengthening this vital component of ICDS.

Recommendations/Observations 
Award scheme for ICDS functionaries  
3.7.1  Anganwadi Workers are the grass root level i mplementers of ICDS Scheme who are honorary workers  from the local 
community. A Scheme of Awards for these workers was introduced by the Government from 2000-01 which includes a national 
level award carrying a cash award of Rs. 25,000/- and a citation and at the State level, a cash award of Rs. 5,000/- and a citation. 
3.7.2 On a specific query in this regard, the Commi ttee was informed that awards for the years 2006-07 , 2007-08 and 2008-09 
were under consideration of the Ministry. Attempt o f the Committee to understand the reasons for this undue delay led to 
another surprising revelation. Process for the awar ds for 2004-05 and 2005-06 started with nominations  being invited from the 
State Governments in August, 2005. It took three an d a half years for awards to be given in February, 2009, reason being late 
receipt of nominations. As a result, selection proc ess for the awardees for 2006-07, 2007-08 and 2008- 09 could be started only 
after February, 2009. It is more than a year since then and names of awardees are yet to be finalized. 
3.7.3 The Committee wonders at the lack of interest  on the part of State Governments in showing a moti vational gesture 
towards their own workers inspite of all the expens es being borne by the Centre. Only effort to be mad e on their part is 
nomination of probable awardees. Awards are to be g iven for services rendered during a particular year . To facilitate a worker 
after such a big gap cannot be considered motivatio nal in any respect. The Committee, accordingly, enj oins upon the Ministry 
to get this process expedited at all the levels and fulfill the objective of this positives initiative. 
Action Taken 3.7.1 to 3.7.3  
  For the awards 2004-05, nominations were invited from the State Governments in August 2005. The Stat es were 
reminded several times for nominations. Due to late receipt of nominations awards for the years 2004-05 and 2005-06 could be 
given only in February 2009. 
  Due to delay in finalizing the awards for 2004-05  and 2005-06, the process to select the awardees for the subsequent years 
i.e.  2006-07, 2007-08 and 2008-09 has been delayed. 
  After issuing of Guidelines by the Central Govern ment, State Governments have to disseminate these a nd obtain 
nominations from projects/districts. Thereafter, th e State Governments have to finalize State Awardees  and was to send 
nominations for National Awards by October 20, 2010 . As on 25.11.2010, only 7 States/UTs Viz: Goa, Him achal Pradesh, 
Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand an d Daman & Diu have sent their nominations for the N ational Level 
Awards. 
  The States/UTs have been asked to expedite the pr ocess and submit their recommendations/nominations 
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee is disappointed with the way the issu e of finalizing the awards for ICDS functionaries i s being 
tackled. Due to delay in finalizing the awards for 2004-05 and 2005-06, the process to select the awar dees for the 
subsequent years i.e.  2006-07, 2007-08 and 2008-09 has been delayed. The  Committee has been informed that after 
issuing of guidelines by the Central Government for finalizing State Awardees, only seven States/UTs viz  Goa, Himachal 
Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Tamil Nadu, Uttar akhand and Daman & Diu have sent their nominations for the 
National Level Awards as on 25 November, 2010. The Committee is of the view that any award has to be announced and 
given at the earliest. Only then, it can be ensured that the awardee has been motivated in the real sense. This fact may be 
impressed upon the concerned State Governments. Procedural constraints leading to undue delay may be identified and 
corrective steps taken accordingly. 
Recommendations/Observations 
Honorarium for Anganwadi Workers and Helpers  
3.8.1 The Committee notes that apart from Rs.1500/-  and 750/- p.m. given to AWWs and Helpers majority of States are giving 
additional honorarium to them. However, NE States/U T like Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Bih ar, Puducherry, 
Gujarat and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have not come forward with such a gesture so far. The Committee desires that the Ministry 

should take up the matter with these States to ensu re better support from them. The Committee has been  voicing its concern 
about these key functionaries of ICDS with manifold activities of not only ICDS remaining under paid inspite of being entrusted 
but also NRHM and other campaigns like Immunization drive etc.  
Recommendations/Observations  
3.8.2 The Committee welcomes the initiatives like p rovision of uniforms for AWWs and Helpers and Insur ance Scheme. 
However, these cannot compensate the low level of h onorarium inspite of being enhanced recently. The f act remains that with 
the cost of living increasing day by day, interest of these grass root level workers performing a very  crucial task in taking care 
of young mothers and little children needs to be given the required importance. For this, more contribution from both the States 
and Centre is required. 
Action, Taken 3.8.1 & 3.8.2  
  The provision of uniforms for Anganwadi Workers [ AWWs] and Anganwadi Helpers [AWHs] under the Scheme  has 
been made with a view to recognize their role and give them an identity. 
  Being honorary workers, AWWs and AWHs are given m onthly honoraria by Govt. of India. Apart from this, many of the 
States have sanctioned additional honoraria. However, the additional honorarium sanctioned by some States/UTs is nominal and 
some States have not sanctioned additional honorari um at all. The States/UT Administrations have been addressed with a 
request to give additional monetary incentives and also pay AWW/ AWH a reasonable amount of additional  honorarium. 
Statement enclosed at Annex.-IV . 
  Besides, States/UTs have been requested to [i] re cruit at least 25% of the Supervisors under the Scheme from AWWs with 
ten years experience of satisfactory service, [ii] engage 25% of AWWs from amongst AWHs having minimum  ten years of 
satisfactory service with requisite qualifications and [iii] consider the services rendered by the AWW s as additional 
qualification for being recruited as Primary School Teachers, ANMs and other such village based posts. 
  All other ICDS functionaries such as the CDPO/DPO /Supervisors etc., are borne on the cadre of the St ate Government. 
The service conditions and salary structure is, therefore, governed by the State Government rules and regulations. However, it is 
seen that there is frequent transfer of the officers looking after ICDS Projects and they too are assigned duties unrelated to ICDS 
Scheme. The State have therefore been requested thr ough various communications by the Ministry to ensu re that these 
functionaries are assigned ICDS work on exclusive b asis to preclude any adverse effect on the implemen tation of the Scheme. 
The issue was also taken up with the States/UTs during the State Secretaries Review Meeting held on 28th October, 2010. 
Comments of the Committee 3.8.1 & 3.8.2  
  The Committee has been informed that only 22 States /UTs have sanctioned additional honoraria for AWWs and 
AWHs. The Committee observes that there are wide di sparities in the quantum of honorarium being given to these 
ICDS functionaries with Rs. 50 being given for AWWs  in Meghalaya to Rs. 2607 being given in Tamil Nadu . Financial 
constraints of State Governments notwithstanding, t he Committee would like to reiterate that the State  Governments 
need to recognize the contribution of grass root le vel workers and give additional monetary incentives and honoraria to 
them. Lack of such an initiative on the part of Sta tes like Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Bihar , Jharkhand, 
Orissa is a cause of serious concern for the Committee as the need of motivated ICDS functionaries in these States is the 
maximum. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take up the issue with the States once again. 
The Committees appreciates the initiative of the Mi nistry against the frequent transfers of officers l ooking after ICDS 
Projects and supports giving of exclusive charge of the ICDS Projects to the officers so that they are  committed towards 
these projects without being diverted by additional workload. The Committee is also of the view that modifications made 
in the recruitment rules so as to ensure better job  opportunities to AWHs and AWWs is a step in the ri ght direction. 
However, the Committee feels that an assessment abo ut the ground realities in this regard at the State  level needs to be 
made.

Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the children of working mothers 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.2  Allocation for this scheme for the year 2009-1 0 was Rs.100.00 crore. Expenditure incurred upto Ja nuary, 2010 is 
Rs.71.97 crore. Budgetary Estimates for the year 20 10-11 for this scheme when compared to last year ha ve been reduced to 
Rs.70.00 crore. On a review of the achievement leve l of the physical targets under the scheme, the Com mittee notes that 
outreach of this scheme has shown no expansion. Number of creches and coverage of children have remained at the same level. 
The Committee has been persistently advocating for expansion of this scheme which is primarily meant to take care of children 
of working mothers with meager income. The Committe e is disturbed to note that instead of increasing, the coverage of this 
scheme has started showing a downward trend. The Co mmittee finds that during 2009-10, against a target  of 31,718 creches, 
only 26,177 creches could be opened up to 31 st Dec ember, 2009. As a result, number of child beneficia ries also stood at 
6,54,425 against a target of 7,92,950 children.  
Recommendations/Observations  
4.3  While trying to analyze the reasons for this r everse progress, Committee’s attention was drawn to  the fact that out of 
31,718 creches covered under the scheme handled by the CSWB and two NOOs, there were complaints agains t the functioning 
of one NGO i.e. Bhartiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh(BAJS S). As a result, control of 5522 creches being run by this NGO was 
temporarily transferred to CSWB on 18th November, 2 008. The Committee is of the view that deficiencies  like improper 
maintenance of records and registers, non-provision  of supplementary nutrition, unsatis-factory covera ge of children, irregular 
payment qf honorarium to creche workers, doctors no t visiting the creches regularly noticed by the mon itoring agencies in the 
creches being run by BAJSS are of a very serious na ture. The Committee finds that inquiry into complaints against the NGO is 
yet to be completed by the Vigilance Wing of the Mi nistry. The Committee is of the firm opinion that t he inquiry should be 
completed at the earliest, followed by action against all the concerned agencies/authorities. 
Action Taken 4.2 & 4.3  
  In 2006, when the “Rajiv Gandhi National Creche S cheme for the Children of Working Mothers” was intr oduced, 12703 
creches were in existence. During 2006-2009, 19015 additional Creches were sanctioned, bringing total number of sanctioned 
creches to 31,718. There has, however, been a reduction in the number of creches due to the following reasons - 
  In November, 2008, 5522 creches earlier run by BA JSS were transferred to CSWB temporarily. However, CSWB was 
able to take over only 3149 creches out of the 5522 creches due to stiff resistance of the creche workers and the functionaries of 
BAJSS. Of these too, only 1221 creches are functional. 
  Consequent to an inspection drive being carried o ut by CSWB, it has also closed down some of its own  creches due to 
poor functioning/non-functioning. Therefore, number of functional creches has further reduced to 22599. 

  Sample inspections of creches by the Ministry hav e also revealed that several of the creches were ei ther non-existent or 
were not functioning. Even in those creches that we re functioning, gaps in provisioning of services li ke SNP, appropriate early 
childhood education, infrastructure etc., were noticed. It was also observed that most of the creches were running for 4-5 hours 
as against the stipulated time of 8 hours. Also sev eral of the children were not of working mothers an d there were a very few 
children of 0-3 years age group. 
  The Ministry, thus, undertook a review of the pro cedures followed by CSWB and ICCW. The review broug ht out that 
whereas in case of ICCW there is some amount of inv olvement of the District Administrations in the sel ection of location, 
management and monitoring of creches, the processes  in both ICCW and CSWB, are largely driven internal ly. It also emerged 
that involvement of the State and District level ad ministrations, at various stages, would help streng then the implementation of 
the scheme and help reach out the benefits to the i ntended beneficiaries. For better implementation of the scheme and ensuring 
delivery of quality services, revised Standard Oper ating Procedure (SOP) has been prepared for CSWB wh ich includes 
enhanced roles for the State Governments/District Administration in the management of creches. 
  Further, the State Governments have been asked to  inspect the creches to assess their quality and al so to assess the 
demand for creches in their States. Any expansion, thus, will be planned and done systematically and c autiously, so that the 
desired quality of services could be provided to the intended beneficiaries. 
  A preliminary enquiry, and thereafter detailed en quiry, was carried out by Chief Vigilance Officers of Ministry of Women 
and Child Development, and the enquiry reports have  been referred to Central Vigilance Commission for advice. Additionally, 
the CCA HRD has also been asked to conduct an audit  of the accounts of BAJSS to verify certain issues brought out in the 
CVO’s enquiry report. The report from CCA is awaited. 
Comments of the Committee 
  The Committee is dismayed to note that the covera ge of Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the Children of 
Working Mothers has been declining mainly due to mi smanagement of creches run by the different impleme nting 
agencies. The Committee finds that out of 5322 crec hes being run by Bhartiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh. CS WB was able 
to take over only 3149 creches due to stiff resista nce of the creche workers and the functionaries of BAJSS and out of 
these creches taken over by CSWB, only 1221 creches  are functional. Another disturbing development is that CSWB 
also had to close down some of its own creches due to poor functioning/non-functional creches. Thus, against the earlier 
figure of total 31,718 functional creches, the numb er of functional creches at present is 22, 599. Eve n in the functional 
creches, sample checks had revealed gaps in provisi oning of services like SNP, appropriate early child hood education, 
infrastructure, non-adherence of stipulated time-period of 8 hours per day. The Committee notes that a fter a review of 
the procedures followed by CSWB and ICCW, the Minis try prepared a revised Standard Operating Procedure  (SOP) 
for CSWB which included enhanced roles for the Stat e Government/District Administration in the managem ent of 
creches and inspection of the creches by the State Governments for assessing their quality and requirement in the States.  
  The Committee has been further informed that a de tailed inquiry of the creches under BAJSS had been carried 
out by the Chief Vigilance Officers of the Ministry  and the enquires reports had been referred to the Central Vigilance 
Commission for advice. The CCA HRD had also been as ked to conduct an audit of the accounts of BAJSS. T he 
Committee would like to be apprised about the detai ls of the reports of the CVOs and the status of rep orts referred to 
the CVC. The Committees feels that the principle of  financial accountability should be upheld. The Com mittee is of the 
view that corrective steps like inquiry, inspection s and audit of accounts of creches taken now have b een over-delayed. 
The Committee hopes that the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) devised by the Ministry with enhanced role for the 
State Governments/District Administration in the ma nagement of creches will prove effective. The Commi ttee is of the 
view that with decline in the coverage of this scheme due to non-functioning and poor functioning of creches, the need of 
the hour is to revitalize the scheme with a pro-act ive role of the Ministry in coordination with the S tate implementing 
agencies and an effective monitoring mechanism in place. 
 
 

Recommendations/Observations  
4.4   The Committee finds that charge of 5522 crech es being run by BAJSS was temporarily transferred t o CSWB on 18th 
November, 2008. It has been more that 16 months since then and CSWB which is already handling 20,893 creches continues to 
have the additional charge of 5522 creches. The Com mittee wonders whether the CSWB has the required ma npower to 
effectively handle the additional responsibility. T he Committee is somewhat surprised to note that as per the Annual Action 
Plan 2010-11, around 26,000 creches benefiting 4,12 ,875 children are targeted to be covered. This targ et shows a considerable 
decline when compared with achievement of 26,177 cr eches with coverage of 6,54,425 children as on 31st  December, 2009. 
This confirms Committee’s apprehensions about 5522 creches earlier run by BAJSS being non-functional. No other plausible 
reason seems to be there for such a situation. The Committee would like to be apprised about the statu s of all the functional 
creches.  
Action Taken  
  As regards handling additional responsibility of running the creches taken over by , CSWB, it is men tioned that CSWB 
implements the scheme through NGGs. These are also supervised by State Social Welfare Boards in every State and through 
their field officers who monitor the functioning th e creches. Therefore, CSWB is in a position to hand le the additional 
responsibility assigned to them. 
  As reported by CSWB, out of 5522 creches, 3149 cr eches were taken over by them but the remaining 2373 creches could 
not be taken over at all due to practical difficult ies like reluctance of BAJSS creche workers to work with CSWB. Out of 3149, 
only 1221 creches are functional. Presently 22599 c reches, which include 1221 creches earlier run by B AJSS, are functional 
which are being run by CSWB and ICCW. 
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee has been informed that functioning of  creches is supervised by the State Social Welfare Boards in 
every State through their field officers who monitor the creches. CSWB being not directly involved in the supervision of 
the creche was in a position to handle the addition al creches run by BAJSS. The Committee is rather su rprised by the 
response of the Ministry as in the previous paras, it has been categorically admitted by it that due t o poor 
functioning/non-functioning of creches under its ch arge, some of them had to be closed down. The Commi ttee can only 
conclude that there were inherent shortcomings in t he creches run by both CSWB and BAJSS which were al lowed to 
continue for long. The Committee would emphasize th at all the corrective measures along with the follo w-up action 
taken on vigilance inquiries should lead to fully operational creches serving the needs of targeted beneficiaries. 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.5  The Committee notes that NIPCCD which was requ ested to prepare a Concept Paper suggesting revisio n in the existing 
scheme with a view to restructure the scheme has submitted the paper on 2nd February, 2010. At present, an internal Committee 
of the Ministry is examining the Report. The Commit tee notes that the Concept Paper has recommended ma jor changes in the 
cost norms, manpower requirement, inclusion of new components like Play and Sleeping Material Kit (PSE Kit), rent for creche 
building, extensive training for the workers and mo nitoring on six monthly basis. The Committee welcom es these suggestions 
for improvement which were long awaited. The Committee would appreciate if the final decision on the Concept Paper is taken 
at the earliest and approval process is also expedited. The Committee notices a major change suggested in the Concept Paper in 
the implementing agencies from CSWB and two NGOs to  SHGs, Mahila Mandals, Women’s Organization Panchay ats and 
Tribal Associations etc. under the super vision of the State Governments. The Committee feels that thi s is a step in the right 
direction. 
Action Taken  
  A Committee was set up in the Ministry to suggest  changes in the RGNCS. In addition to increase in e xpenditure and 
staffing norms, the Committee has also recommended changes in the process of selection of location/cre che workers/ NGOs, 
more stringent monitoring procedures and enhanced r ole for the State Government! District Administrati ons so that the quality 

of services could be maintained to the desired stan dards. Based on the report submitted by this Commit tee, a revised scheme is 
being formulated and will be submitted for necessary approval.  
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee is of the view that the process of the revised scheme of RGNCS being formulated at present should 
be expedited so that a fully approved scheme is in place for the targeted beneficiaries. 
VI.  INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.3  BE 2009-10 of Rs. 60.00 crore for the Scheme w as reduced to Rs. 50.00 crore at the RE stage. This  reduction was 
because most of the States signed the MOU in the se cond half of the financial year 2009-10 and submitt ed their proposal 
thereafter. As a result, only Rs. 3.00 crore could be released by the Ministry by the end of January, 2010. As per the latest 
information furnished by the Ministry, central shar e of Grant-in-aid of Rs. 33.31 crore to 14 States f or implementation of the 
Scheme and Rs. 9.33 crore to the Child line India F oundation, Mumbai for running the Child line servic e in the country has 
been released. 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.4  The Committee notes that against a projected r equirement of Rs.400 crore, Rs.300 crore has been a llocated for the 
Scheme in 2010-11 mainly for the setting up of Juve nile Justice Board and Child Welfare Committee, Spe cial Juvenile Police 
Units, Child Protection Societies and Open Shelters , Child Line Service in 163 cities in the country f or 300 districts of 25 
States/UTs. The Committee appreciates the lofty tar gets set for the implementation of the Scheme. Howe ver, getting the 
remaining States/UTs to sign the MOU specially due to the Scheme being on a cost sharing basis and set ting up of Juvenile 
Justice Board, Child Welfare Committees, Special Juvenile Police Units, Child Protection Services in 300 districts of at least 25 
States would not be an easy task. Besides that, imp lementation of the Scheme in the 17 States which ha ve signed the MoU will 
also have to be closely monitored, so .as to tackle  the initial problem areas. The Committee hopes tha t the assurance of the 
Ministry with regard to the speedy and accelerated implementation of the scheme holds true. 
Action Taken 6.3 & 6.4  
  The Ministry has been providing hand-holding supp ort to the States for handling initial teething tro ubles in 
implementation of the scheme. Regional consultation s have been organised wherein the doubts and diffic ulties are ironed out 
and the States are encouraged to share their experi ences and best practices. Besides, to appraise the financial proposals for 
release of grants under the scheme and review the p rogress of implementation, a Project Approval Board  has been constituted 
under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Ministry of Wo men & Child Development, with members from various Ministries and 
Departments. In addition, meetings are held with th e implementing officers of the State Government to help them frame their 
action plans and financial proposals. 
  These interactions with the State Governments ind icate that they are taking some time to build a per spective on how the 
child protection network should be strengthened and  expanded in their States. There is, thus, a time l ag of 5-8 months between 
signing of MOU and submission of financial proposal s. Also even in those cases where proposals have be en received (from 18 
.States up to 25th November 2010), many of them are  incomplete. The States are being asked to assess t he available resources 
and actual requirements and frame their proposal based on identified additional needs. 
  In 2010-11, up to 25th November 2010, proposals w orth Rs. 43.11 crores have been approved for 07 Sta tes namely, 
Mizoram, Tamil Nadu, Bihar, Gujarat, West Bengal, A ssam and Orissa, and Rs.24.58 crore have been relea sed to them as the 
first installment. In addition, Rs.7.89 crores has been released to CIF, Mumbai for running Childline services across the country. 
  In the 29 States, having 546 districts, which hav e signed the MOU so far, CWCs have been set up in 465 districts, JJBs in 
445 and SJPUs in 478. Setting up of other structure s, such as the Societies at State and District levels, State Adoption Resource 
Agencies etc., is in process in these States and it is expected that all these structures will be in place by 2011-12. 
 

Comments of the Committee 
  The Committee has been informed that twenty nine States/UTs have signed the MOU for implementation o f the 
Integrated Child Protection Scheme. A project Appro val Board has been constituted under the Chairmansh ip of 
Secretary, Ministry of WCD to appraise the financia l proposals for release of grants under the scheme and review the 
progress of implementation. Proposals worth Rs. 43. 11 crores have been approved for seven States uptil l 25 November, 
2010 and Rs 24.58 crore have been released to them as the first installment. Out of the total 546 dist ricts in 29 States, 
Child Welfare Committees have been set up in 465 districts, Juvenile Justice Boards in 445 districts and Special Juvenile 
Police units in 478 districts. While appreciating t he increasing number of State Governments signing t he MOU for the 
scheme, the Committee believes that an uphill task is yet to be completed. The State Governments need to put in place 
the child protection network like Juvenile Justice Boards, Child Welfare Committee, Special Juvenile P olice Units etc 
for effective implementation of the scheme. The Com mittee is happy to note that the Ministry is extend ing its 
cooperation to the .States in framing financial pro posals and also assessing their available resources  and actual 
requirements. The Committee recommends that setting up of other structures such as the Societies at St ate and district 
levels, State Adoption Resource Agencies etc in the  States should be expedited so that these agencies are ready for 
implementation of the scheme. An inbuilt effective monitoring mechanism should also be evolved so that  the scheme

VII.   SCHEME OF HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN 
Recommendations/Observations  
7.5  The Committee observes that the process of rev amping of Working Women’s Hostel Scheme started in the first year of 
the Eleventh Plan i.e. 2007.08. After consultation with various stake holders, a draft EFC Memo was ci rculated in June, 2008 
and the EFC meeting was held in October, 2008. Ther eafter, with the approval of the MOS(IC), Ministry of Women and Child 
Development to the recommendations of the EFC, appr oval of the Ministry of Finance was sought in Janua ry, 2009. The 
Ministry of Finance approved the scheme in July, 20 09 with the condition that only projects to be cons tructed on public land 
would be supported under the scheme and eligibility  criteria for inmates, in terms of their gross inco me would be retained. 
Since, there were certain ambiguities in the stated  conditions, Ministry of Law and Justice and therea fter, Ministry of Finance 
were consulted for clarification which has been rec eived in the Ministry in January, 2010. However, am biguities still remain in 
regard to the definition of ‘Public Land”. The matt er is currently under scrutiny in the Ministry. A f inal view will be taken on 
this issue shortly after which revised guidelines o f the revamped scheme would be notified during the 1st quarter of the 
financial year 2010-11. 
Action Taken  
  The issue of “Public Land” has now been clarified  and the revised scheme is being notified. 
Recommendations/Observations  
7.6  The Committee is of the view that three years of the Eleventh Plan are already over and the proce ss of revision of the 
Scheme still remains incomplete. Concerted efforts have to be made to, overcome procedural difficultie s and ambiguities. The 
Committee hopes that with new components of mainten ance grants, grant for hostels in rented buildings,  accreditation of PG 
like accommodation, grant for initial furnishing et c., the revamped Schemed will go a long way in reac hing the targeted 
beneficiaries in the real sense. The Committee is a lso happy to note that under the new Scheme, endeav or would be to 
streamline the process of scrutiny and approvals so  that the time-lag between the receipt of applicati ons and their 
approval/rejection is cut down significantly. The C ommittee would also like to point out that a mechan ism whereby both 
surprise and regular inspections of functional hostels are carried out, needs to be evolved. This would ensure that the Scheme is 
benefiting the targeted beneficiaries.  

Action Taken  
  The Ministry is now developing a proposal for reg ular inspections of all the schemes. 
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee has been monitoring the implementation of the Scheme of Hostels for Working Women for the last 
many years. The Scheme has never been implemented a s envisaged due to inherent problem areas and opera tional 
difficulties. Unfortunately, the process of revisio n of scheme has been unduly long with almost an ent ire plan period 
being spent therefor. As per the latest feedback ma de available to the Committee, the last ambiguity i n the revised 
scheme, i.e.  definition of the tern ‘Public Land’ has been clar ified and the revised scheme is being notified. The  
Committee hopes that by the end of 2010-11, it woul d be notified so that it may become operational fro m the beginning 
of 2011-12 itself. 
VIII.  CARA 
Recommendations/Observations  
8.4  The Committee has been informed that the guide lines for in-country and inter-country adoptions of  2004 and 2006 
respectively are under the process of revision and at present an Expert Committee has been appointed by Ministry to finalize the 
same. The Committee hopes that the hindrances faced  by CARA at present in cases of inter-country adopt ion like judicial

  Though the guidelines for in-country and inter-co untry adoptions are under revision, the hindrances face4 in the adoption

Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee would like to emphasize that the proc ess for having an enabling legislation for the Hagu e 
Convention on Inter-country Adoptions should be expedited so as to ensure removal of all procedural delays being faced 
in the adoption of children.

Recommendations/Observations

scheme. It has been reported that 15 NGOs were blac klisted under RMK during 2008-09 and 79 NGOs were b lacklisted during

Also, strict monitoring of the NGOs should be an im portant component for the real assessment of the pe rformance level of the 
scheme. The Ministry is contemplating to adopt the system of on-line monitoring of the projects sancti oned. The Committee

XII.  NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW) 
Recommendations/Observations  
12.1  The National Commission for Women (NCW) set u p in 1992 is a statutory apex national level body u nder the National 
Commission for Women Act, 1990. NCW reviews the provisions relating to the safeguards for women under the Constitution as 
well as in other laws. it takes up petitions from w omen for redressal of their grievances, and does pr omotional research for the 
advancement of women, takes suo moto  notice of matters relating to deprivation of women ’s rights etc. and takes up the issues 
with appropriate authorities. 
Recommendations/Observations  
12.2  The Committee is aware that the National Commission for Women is the only national level authority having the mandate 
of protecting the rights of women across the country. The most crucial task assigned to the Commission is to investigate specific 
problems or situations arising out of discriminatio n/atrocities against women. However, the Committee feels that the 
Commission has not succeeded fully in carrying out this mandate. This is borne out by the status of co mplaints received by the 
Commission. As per the information made available t o the Committee, out of 15,854 complaints registere d with the 
Commission during 2007-08 and 12,895 complaints dur ing 2008-09, 1781 and 1166 complaints are pending r espectively. The 
Committee finds the details of complaints on which Action Taken Reports from concerned authorities are still pending as more 
disturbing. Out of 8640 and 7509 complaints registe red in 2007-08 and 2008-09 respectively, ATRs, are pending on 5610 and 
4679 complaints respectively. This clearly shows th at the matter has not proceeded beyond the complain t registered with the 
Commission and sent to the concerned authorities for necessary action. 
  Therefore, it would not be wrong to conclude that  no relief whatsoever has been provided to the victim in such a case. The 
very fact that a very large number of complaints fr om 2007-08 and 2008-09 continue to remain pending d efeats the very 
purpose of mandate of safeguarding the rights and interests of women folk of the country, with which the Commission has been 
entrusted. The Committee can well imagine the fate of 13,696 complaints registered with NCW (as on 31. 01.2010) during 
2009-10. The Committee strongly feels that the Nati onal Commission for Women needs to be empowered so as to be in a 
position to take conclusive action incases relating to redressal of grievances received from victims.

(ix) Shortage of Staff: There is no permanent staff  in NCW. The change of staff occurs frequently due to lack of 
permanent vacancy, which leads to break in continuity leading to delays in finalization. 
NCW has been requested to suggest a restructuring proposal for examining their staffing requirement. 
Comments of the Committee  
  The Committee takes note of the problems encountere d by the NCW in disposal of complaints registered a t the 
agency. Given the increase in the number of complai nts filed, a restructuring proposal for examining t he staffing

an important role in redressal of grievances of wom en suffering various kinds of atrocities and theref ore it needs to 
widen its scope and structure so as to strengthen i t for efficient disposal of complaints. There shoul d be an increase in 
the number of staff including the counsellors who have to deal with ever increasing complaints due to introduction of the 
system of online filing of complaints. The Committee is of the view that adequate allocation of funds along with increase 
in the number of staff should be taken up by the Ministry on a priority basis.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS – AT A GLANCE  
II.  BUDGERARY ALLOCATION 
  The Committee has been given to understand that t he procedural delay in approvals of new schemes lik e Rajiv 
Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls (RGSEAG), Relief to and Rehabilitation of Rape Victims, Indira 
Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana and the National Miss ion for Empowerment of Women was the main reason fo r 
delayed initiation and implementation of the schemes. Analysis of these five schemes clearly indicates that procedure for 
completion of various formalities is a protracted e xercise which may continue for years with either th e scheme being 
completely dropped or being approved with entirely different norms. Scheme for Relief to and Rehabilit ation of Rape 
Victims was framed by the National Commission for W omen 15 years ago, that too on the direction of Sup reme Court. 
After several rounds of discussion, it was on the 7 th March, 2010, the Expenditure Finance Committee h ad 
recommended a scheme with a different nomenclature to be implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme d uring the 
Eleventh Plan. Last quarter of the Financial Year 2 010-11 has already commenced and with only one year  of the Plan 
period remaining, the scheme is yet to be launched,  reason being all the procedural formalities not completed even now. 
For the other two schemes; i.e. Rajiv Gahdhi Scheme  for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls and Indira Gan dhi 
Matritva Sahyog Yojana, although approval has been given by the competent authority for implementation  in 200 and 
52 selected districts on 25 March, 2010 and 25 May,  2010 respectively, no feedback is there about the launch of these 
schemes on pilot basis. 
  Fate of Swayamsidha Phase-II is not only somewhat  surprising but also disturbing, a scheme whose Pha se-I was 
successfully implemented by the Ministry. For two years, implementation of this scheme remained suspended and in the 
third year, it was decided not to pursue the scheme , as another Ministry has launched a similar progra mme on a bigger 
scale. The Committee would like to remind the Minis try about its observation made few years ago for un dertaking a 
review of all its women-specific schemes where over -lapping was there both intra- Ministry and inter-M inistries. The 
Committee would like to be apprised about the comments of the Planning Commission and the details of the programme 
of Ministry of Rural Development and also the areas of overlap of both the schemes. The Committee would like to point 
out that Swayamsidha is a flagship programme of the  Ministry for holistic empowerment of women through  SHGs 
covering all districts/blocks in the country. Further, the World Bank intends to fund its several components which works 
out to about 50 per cent of total costs. In view of  this, the Committee wonders whether components of the scheme with 
the objective of women empowerment through SHGs wou ld be achieved through the other scheme of the Mini stry of 
Rural Development. 
  The Committee is also not very hopeful about the early start about the National Mission for Empowerm ent of 
Women. The Committee would like to be apprised abou t whether the process of creation of posts for Miss ion 
Directorate and National Resource Centre for Women has been completed. It would also like to know about the number 
of States which have set up State Resource Centres for Women uptil now.  (Para 2.6)  
  The Committee is not convinced by the justificati on given by the Ministry about the pendency of Util isation 
Certificates dating back to 1986-87 onwards. Latest status of Utilisation Certificates also does not indicate a satisfactory 
position. The Committee would appreciate if pro-active efforts are initiated by the Ministery for liquidating the very old 
Utilization Certificates. Simultaneously, pendency pertaining to the recent years also needs to be bro ught to the 
minimum level. The Committee is of the view that ad herence to financial norms by the implementing agen cies needs to 
be impressed upon emphatically. Continuance of pending Utilisation Certificates only indicates that the various schemes 
meant for the welfare of children and women, the most vulnerable sections of the society are not being implemented in a 
time-bound manner.   (Para 2.8)  
  The Committee does not wish to be drawn in techni cal/procedural formalities pertaining to pendency o f unspent 
balances. Committee’s prime concern is for implemen tation of a major programme meant for children in a  judicious 
manner as per the envisaged norms and action plan. States-wise excess expenditure/unspent balance as o n 31 March, 
2010 confirms Committee’s justified concern. There are states like Gujarat (Rs. 24.61 crore), Haryana (Rs. 67.92 crore), 

Jharkhand (Rs. 47.37 crore), Kerala (Rs. 44.07 cror e), Tamil Nadu (Rs. 39.27 crore), West Bengal (Rs. 74.60 crore) 
which have incurred excess expenditure. In contrast , States like Bihar (Rs. 13.11 crore), Orissa (Rs. 28.50 crore), 
Rajasthan (Rs. 18.32 crore), Uttar Pradesh (Rs. 47.18 crore), Assam (Rs. 26.28 crore) and Nagaland (Rs. 16.22 crore) are 
having unspent balance. Either way, it can be concl uded that the Flagship Scheme of ICDS is both not r eaching all its 
targeted beneficiaries and not being implemented as  per the financial norms. The Committee, therefore,  reiterates that

required corrective measures.  (Para 2.9)
